title: ArrayPool and MemoryPool (reuse buffers without LOH churn)
hook: Renting a buffer from ArrayPool reuses an existing array instead of allocating a new Large Object Heap (LOH) object every request. MemoryPool gives you an IMemoryOwner for the same pattern with Span-friendly semantics.

blocks.text: System.Buffers.ArrayPool<T> maintains pools of arrays that callers rent and return. Rent(minimumLength) may return an array larger than requested — always track the length you actually need. System.Buffers.MemoryPool<T> provides IMemoryOwner<T> wrappers with deterministic disposal. Both patterns avoid per-request LOH allocations for CSV parsing, HTTP body buffering, and serialization scratch space.

entries.plainDefinition: Shared pool of reusable arrays; Rent returns, Return gives back.
entries.example: ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(90_000) for a CSV row buffer.

entries.plainDefinition: Pool that returns IMemoryOwner<T> for Span/Memory-based APIs.
entries.example: MemoryPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(4096) returns a disposable memory block.

entries.plainDefinition: Disposable wrapper around a rented memory block; Dispose returns it to the pool.

blocks.text: A CSV import service allocating new byte[90_000] per row hits the LOH and triggers expensive generation-2 collections. Renting from ArrayPool reuses the same backing array across requests, slashing allocation rate and LOH fragmentation. The tradeoff: you must Return arrays (or Dispose IMemoryOwner) and never use a returned buffer after returning it.

blocks.title: When to pool
blocks.body: Pool when buffers are large (near LOH threshold), short-lived, and same-sized across requests. Do not pool tiny arrays — the bookkeeping cost exceeds the savings.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Rent from pool
items.body: Get an existing array (possibly larger than requested) from the shared pool.

items.title: Use only needed length
items.body: Track actual bytes written; the rented array may be oversized.

items.title: Return or Dispose
items.body: ArrayPool.Return or IMemoryOwner.Dispose puts the buffer back.

items.title: Never touch after return
items.body: Another thread may rent the same array — use-after-return is a data race.

snippet.label: Verify pooling reduced LOH pressure
snippet.code:
dotnet-counters monitor -p <pid> \
  System.Runtime[alloc-rate,gc-heap-size,gen-2-gc-count]
# Before pooling: alloc-rate high, gen-2 spikes per CSV batch
# After pooling: alloc-rate drops, gen-2 stable
snippet.explanation: Compare alloc-rate and gen-2-gc-count before and after introducing ArrayPool on the hot path.

blocks.title: Buffer reuse patterns
rows: No built-in equivalent; reuse a module-level Buffer
Buffer.allocUnsafe reuses but no size bucket

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Returning a buffer then continuing to read it. Renting tiny arrays where allocation cost is negligible. Storing a rented array in a field beyond the request scope. Forgetting clearArray: true for buffers holding secrets.

blocks.text: ArrayPool<T>.Shared buckets arrays by size power-of-two. Rent may return an array up to 2× the minimum length — always use a length variable, never buffer.Length as the data size. MemoryPool<T> wraps the same idea with IMemoryOwner for APIs that accept Memory<T>. Pooling trades allocation for complexity: use-after-return bugs, data leakage between tenants if clearArray is false, and oversized arrays wasting cache lines. How to prove it in production: dotnet-counters alloc-rate and gen-2-gc-count drop after pooling a CSV or HTTP buffering hot path.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Cannot exceed ~1 KB safely; no async escape

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Pooling every allocation including tiny ones, or returning a buffer then passing it to another async continuation. Strong answer: pool large short-lived buffers near LOH threshold; track actual length; Return in finally; clear sensitive data.

interviewTakeaways: ArrayPool rents reusable arrays; MemoryPool returns IMemoryOwner for Span/Memory-based APIs.
Do not pool tiny arrays — the bookkeeping exceeds savings; target LOH-sized buffers.
For CSV imports and HTTP buffering, pool 85 KB+ buffers and verify alloc-rate drops with dotnet-counters.
60s: Rent from ArrayPool, use only needed length, Return in finally. MemoryPool for IMemoryOwner. Avoids LOH churn. Never use after return.
Follow-up: what happens if you forget clearArray: true on a buffer holding PII?
commonPitfalls: Pooling every allocation including 16-byte arrays — gets you rejected because pool overhead exceeds savings.
Strong answer: pool large short-lived buffers near LOH threshold; track actual length; Return in finally.
Using a returned buffer after Return — another request may overwrite your data.
Assuming Rent returns exactly the requested size — it may return a larger power-of-two bucket.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node has no ArrayPool. Developers reuse module-level Buffer objects manually. C# ArrayPool provides thread-safe bucketing and clear-on-return semantics.
new Uint8Array(90000) in TS allocates on the V8 heap every time. C# ArrayPool<byte>.Rent avoids a new LOH object per call.
